name: Kentucky

notes: Food for home is exempt (KRS 139.485); candy, soft drinks and prepared food are taxed at 6%, which is not counted here.

Alcohol is taxed at 6%, on top of an 11% wholesale tax on spirits and 10% on wine and beer (KRS 243.884), left out here. Smaller wet cities and some counties charge a regulatory license fee on alcohol sales of up to 5% (some older fees are higher; KRS 243.075). It is a percent of the seller's retail receipts, so the rule here would count it, but each city and county sets its own fee and no list of who charges what has been compiled, so it isn't counted yet (on the follow-up list).

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at 6%, on top of excise taxes left out here: $1.10 a pack of cigarettes, 15% of the wholesale price on most other tobacco and on open vapor systems (snuff and chewing tobacco by the unit), and $1.50 a closed vapor cartridge.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed; massage, tanning, tattooing and some other personal services are (KRS 139.200), which is not counted here.
Laundry and dry cleaning are taxed since July 1, 2018 (KRS 139.200(2)(l)); coin-operated laundry isn't.
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and taxed by the gallon instead (26.4 cents from July 1, 2026, under an emergency rule), left out here.
Auto repair labor: labor to install parts sold in the same repair job is taxed; labor alone, with no parts sold, isn't.
Hotel stays pay a 1% state transient room tax on top of the 6% sales tax, plus local room taxes of 3% to 4% and special taxes (Louisville 8.5%), which are not counted here.
Kentucky has no sales tax holiday.
Kentucky extended its sales tax to many services in 2018 and 2022-2023 (KRS 139.200); the services below are from state law.
gaps: Kentucky has no local general sales tax; the 6% state rate applies everywhere. Cities that were fourth or fifth class in 2014 may levy a restaurant tax of up to 3% (KRS 91A.400); the Department for Local Government's registry lists the 222 cities allowed to, not which of them do, and gives no rates. The taxes of 41 cities whose own code, page or tourist commission gives the current rate are counted in their restaurant rates; the other cities on the Kentucky League of Cities' 2021 list of cities with a restaurant tax, and taxes reported since, are noted on their pages, not counted. The registry's other cities, not on that list, are noted as allowed to levy one, and each says what was found: no levy in the codes of ordinances of 72 (tables of special ordinances included, since Morgantown's tax sits only in one); for 38 more, the latest filing of the tourist commission covering them with the Department for Local Government shows only a room tax, or only another city's restaurant tax; 41 have no registered commission (most likely no tax, though the registry is incomplete); for 14 the commission's filings don't name its taxes. Hotel and motel taxes, and the regulatory license fees that smaller wet cities and some counties charge on alcohol sales (up to 5%, some older ones higher; KRS 243.075), are not counted.

warn.text: Bardstown draws many visitors (its bourbon distilleries and My Old Kentucky Home), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (0.3%) and its 37 lodging places (1.9 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, though 2 of its 4 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Calvert City may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels along Interstate 24 (6 lodging places, 2.6 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Mount Vernon may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its hotels and motels along Interstate 75 (11 lodging places, 3.4 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Audubon Park's page is built from a census tract it shares with Louisville; that tract may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its airport hotels (8 lodging places, 2.9 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers rather than tourists, so read that flag with care.

Forest Hills' page is built from a census tract it shares with Jeffersontown; that tract's flag as a visitor economy rests on its 8 lodging places (2.2 per 1,000 residents), in a suburban area that isn't a tourist destination, so read that flag with care.

Maytown's flag as a visitor economy may come only from homes the Census counts as seasonal (146 of 1,175 in its census tract, 12.4%), which may be hunting or weekend places rather than tourism; read that flag with care.

Muldraugh's flag as a visitor economy rests on its 5 lodging places (4.4 per 1,000 residents), next to Fort Knox, an Army post; they likely serve people traveling to the post more than tourists, so read that flag with care.
